The chips wear out in six years. The debt runs for decades.

Michael WangWorking paper and open dataset, version 2026.10.15Updated weekly from SEC EDGAR
  • Meta Platforms
  • Alphabet
  • Amazon
  • Oracle
  • Microsoft
  • CoreWeave

Abstract

Since January 2024, five of the largest spenders on AI infrastructure have raised $383 billion in bonds and loans. We assemble every tranche from 36 SEC filings (159 tranches), extract terms with a language model, and verify each one against finance identities. Matching each tranche to the depreciation life its issuer discloses for servers (5–6 years), we find that 73% of the principal falls due after that hardware is fully depreciated. The amount-weighted median maturity is Nov 2035. The result survives much longer asset lives: at ten years, 51% still outlives the asset; at twenty, 34%. Credit markets price most issuers at or inside the investment-grade index. The exception is Oracle, whose ten-year new-issue spread widened by 50 basis points while the index moved -18. On the asset side, capital spending is outgrowing the cloud revenue it is meant to earn, Oracle covers its interest only 4.5× from operating income, and the companies have signed a further $1.15T of data-center leases that are not yet on their balance sheets.

Key findings

  1. $383.3B raised since 2024; $246.2B of it in 2026 alone. Fig. 2
  2. 73% is owed after the servers it financed are written off; one bond runs to 2126. Fig. 1, 12
  3. Robust to asset life: 51% at 10 years, 34% at 20. Fig. 13, Table 3
  4. Oracle pays +50bp more than in 2024 for ten-year money; the market average fell. Fig. 4, 5
  5. Capex is 174% of operating cash flow at Oracle and 337% at CoreWeave. Fig. 6
  6. Signed leases not yet on the balance sheet total $1.15T, 3.0× the bonds. Table 2
  7. Capex is growing faster than cloud revenue: Oracle +162% vs +39%, Microsoft +80% vs Azure +41%. Fig. 9
  8. Interest coverage: Oracle 4.5×, CoreWeave -0.1×; the other four at least 28×. Fig. 10
  9. Only 4% of the debt names AI in its use of proceeds. Method
  • Servers it financed still in service
  • Debt still owed after they are written off
  • Half of all principal is due after this date

The sample

The sample covers every bond and loan priced since 1 January 2024 by the six companies whose capital spending is most concentrated in AI data centers. Microsoft is included as a control: it borrowed nothing in public markets over the period. Table 1 summarises the 159 tranches that enter the totals.

1How much they have borrowed

Since January 2024, the five companies spending most aggressively on AI have sold 159 bonds and loans worth $383.3B, across 33 separate deals.

The pace is accelerating. They borrowed $16.8B in 2024 and $120.4B in 2025. In 2026, with the year not yet over, the figure is $246.2B.

The largest single day: Amazon raised $37.0B on Mar 10, 2026, split across 11 separate bonds.

CoreWeave is the smallest borrower here and the most dependent on it. It has no investment-grade rating, so its $40.6B comes as high-yield bonds paying up to 9.75%, convertibles, and $19.8B of loans secured by the GPUs themselves.

2Who is borrowing, and how

Each circle is one deal: every bond a company priced on a single day. Its area is proportional to the amount raised. Hover for the terms; click to open the filing.

The US market was not big enough. 20% of the money, $78.0B, was raised in euros, sterling, Canadian dollars and yen. That includes Alphabet's £1 billion bond due in 2126: a hundred-year loan to fund a five-year asset.

CoreWeave borrows differently. Its deals are term loans secured by GPUs and customer contracts, convertibles, and high-yield notes. These are instruments built for companies that lenders consider risky.

One company is missing. Microsoft, among the largest AI spenders, has not sold a bond since 2024, and its total debt fell from $49.8B to $40.3B. Its finance leases, mostly data centers it rents rather than owns, rose from $14.9B to $66.6B. That is leverage too, just not in this chart.

3What lenders charge

Bond investors have been relaxed about all this. The extra yield they demand to hold an average investment-grade corporate bond instead of Treasuries has stayed low, at about 0.78 percentage points.

Each dot is a new ten-year bond from one of these companies, at the spread it paid over Treasuries on the day it was sold. Meta, Alphabet and Amazon borrow at or below the market average.

Oracle is the exception. Its ten-year spread rose from 95 basis points in Sep 2024 to 145 in Feb 2026, while the market average fell from 92 to 74. Lenders are charging Oracle for its AI bet.

New-issue spreads are measured against a single Treasury benchmark; the indices are option-adjusted spreads across thousands of bonds. The comparison shows direction, not a precise premium.

A single tenor can mislead, because longer bonds always pay more. Figure 5 fits each issuer's full credit curve: the spread it pays at every maturity. Between 2024–25 and 2026 every issuer's fitted ten-year spread rose (Amazon +23bp, Alphabet +18bp, Meta Platforms +10bp). Oracle's rose most, by 47bp, from 95 to 142. Because the whole curve moved, a shift in the mix of maturities cannot explain it.

4Why they need to borrow

Why borrow at all? Capital spending, the claret line, has more than doubled in two years at every company here. The black line is the cash the businesses actually generate. Shading marks spending beyond it. The blue dashes show total debt.

Amazon spent 94% of its operating cash flow on capital projects in fiscal 2025, leaving almost nothing for anything else.

Oracle and CoreWeave spend far more than they earn. Oracle's fiscal 2026 capital spending was 174% of its operating cash flow; CoreWeave's was 337%. The gap is borrowed.

Microsoft's spending is covered by its cash flow, which is why it can build without new bonds, though it leans on leases instead.

5Where the money goes, and whether it comes back

Figure 6 shows annual totals. This chapter follows the money quarter by quarter: how much is spent (Figure 7), how the shortfall is filled (Figure 8), what the spending is earning (Figure 9), whether the debt can be serviced (Figure 10), and what the spending will cost in depreciation (Figure 11). All figures come from the companies' 10-Q and 10-K filings; every number links back to its filing in the downloadable data.

In their latest reported quarters, capital spending equalled 147% of revenue at Oracle and 249% at CoreWeave, against 38% at Alphabet and 27% at Amazon.

Where does the money come from? Figure 8 starts from cash generated by operations, subtracts capital spending, dividends and buybacks, and shows how what is left (or missing) was covered: new debt, cash on hand, or other flows. In fiscal 2026 Oracle was $29.6B short and raised $39.2B of net debt. Meta, by contrast, had $14.5B left over in fiscal 2025 and still borrowed $29.9B.

Is the spending paying for itself? Figure 9 compares the growth of capital spending with the growth of the revenue it is meant to earn. Each company's cloud figure is what it discloses: AWS and Google Cloud revenue, Oracle's cloud revenue, Microsoft's Azure growth rate (Microsoft does not report Azure in dollars), all of CoreWeave's revenue, and for Meta, which has no cloud business, total revenue. In the latest fiscal year, capex grew faster than cloud revenue at five of the six: Oracle +162% against +39%, Microsoft +80% against Azure +41%, Meta +87% against revenue +22%.

Can they service it? Interest coverage divides operating income over the last four quarters by interest expense. For Meta, Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft it is at least 28×. Oracle's is 4.5×. CoreWeave's operating income is close to zero, so its coverage is -0.1×: it pays its interest from new borrowing and operating cash, not from profit.

The bill for the hardware arrives as depreciation. Figure 11 spreads each year's capex over the server life the company discloses (using the life in force when it was bought) and the rest over twenty years, then projects forward from capex already spent, with no further spending. It is an illustration, not a forecast: the split between servers and buildings is not disclosed, so it is a slider. Even on spending already made, CoreWeave's depreciation would reach about 46% of its latest annual revenue.

Not all of the AI build-out is financed with bonds. The companies have also signed data-center leases that have not yet started and so are not on their balance sheets. Together these come to $1.15T, 3.0 times the bonds and loans in this tracker. They are not counted in the headline total.

6The mismatch

Here is the catch. Every company in this story tells its auditors that AI servers stay useful for 5 to 6 years. That is the claret bar: their own estimate, from their annual reports.

The blue bar is how long the money is owed, on average, weighted by size. At Meta it is 20 years. At Alphabet, 17.

At the far end are 40-year bonds from Meta and Oracle, 50 from Amazon, and Alphabet's 100-year bond. In all, 73% of this debt is still owed after the hardware it paid for has been written off.

CoreWeave is the exception: its loans are sized to the life of the GPUs, which is also why they cost so much more.

Figure 12 compares averages. Figure 13 follows the money through time instead. Suppose each tranche paid for servers of equal cost, bought on the day it was priced and depreciated straight-line. The claret area is the book value those servers still have; the blue line is the debt still owed. Once the claret runs out, every remaining dollar of debt is backed by nothing that it bought.

Server lives are an accounting estimate, and part of this money funds buildings and power that last far longer. Move the slider to test the claim. Even with a twenty-year life, 34% of the principal is still owed after the asset is written off (Table 3).

The bill arrives in waves. Most of this debt falls due after 2032, the year by which every server bought so far will be fully depreciated. By then the companies will need new hardware, and will still be paying for the old.

Not counted here: debt that stays off the balance sheet

In October 2025 Meta set up a joint venture to build its Louisiana data center campus. Partners fund most of the roughly $27B cost, Meta keeps 20% and leases the buildings back on 4-year initial terms. Because Meta does not control the venture, none of that borrowing appears in its debt. Its own filing puts Meta's maximum exposure at $45.95B, including residual value guarantees of about $28B.

“Our maximum exposure to loss related to the Venture was $ 45.95 billion as of December 31, 2025”Meta Platforms, 10-K for 2025

7Objections, and what the data says

A mismatch between asset life and debt maturity is not the same as a default. Here are the strongest counter-arguments and how far the evidence goes.

“These bonds are backed by the whole company, not by servers.”
True. They are senior unsecured obligations, serviced from total cash flow, and for Meta, Alphabet and Amazon that cash flow is large (Figure 6). The finding is about timing: when the servers are obsolete, the same cash flow must pay for their replacements and keep servicing the debt that bought them. That matters most where capex already exceeds operating cash, which today means Oracle and CoreWeave.
“Not all of it buys servers. Buildings and power last decades.”
Also true, and the filings do not split the proceeds. Table 3 brackets the answer: even if every dollar bought assets lasting twenty years, 34% of the principal would still be owed after they were written off. With thirty years, 25% would be.
“Investment-grade companies always issue long bonds.”
They do, which is why the comparison is with the assets, not with other bonds. Corporate-finance theory predicts that firms match debt maturity to asset life (Myers 1977; Hart and Moore 1994), and the evidence broadly supports it (Stohs and Mauer 1996). Here the asset is unusually short-lived, so the usual long-bond habit produces an unusually large gap.
“Useful lives are estimates. GPUs may last longer.”
Possibly, though the companies themselves disagree about the direction. Meta lengthened its server lives to 5.5 years in 2025, while Amazon shortened a subset from six years to five. The sliders in Figure 13 and Figure 11 let readers set their own estimate.
“Spreads are tight. Lenders are not worried.”
For most issuers that is what the data shows (Figures 4 and 5), although every issuer's curve drifted up in 2026. Oracle stands out: it now pays about 50 basis points more for ten-year money than in Sep 2024, while the market average fell.

How this was made

What counts

Every bond and loan sold since January 2024 by six companies whose capital spending is dominated by AI data centers: Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, Oracle, Microsoft and CoreWeave. Their filings mostly say proceeds are for “general corporate purposes”, so we cannot prove each dollar went to AI. We count it anyway and say so: this is money raised by AI's biggest spenders, not money legally earmarked for AI. Only $16.8B (4%) comes with use-of-proceeds language that names AI, GPUs or data centers.

Revolving credit lines are listed but not counted, because they are commitments rather than borrowing. Delayed-draw term loans are counted at their full committed size. Off-balance-sheet structures and leases are discussed but not counted. Non-dollar bonds are converted at the Federal Reserve's H.10 exchange rate on the pricing date.

How the data is built

  1. SEC filings36 term sheets and 8-Ks
  2. LLM extractionterms plus a verbatim quote
  3. Finance checksspread = yield − Treasury; price → yield
  4. Dataset159 tranches, CC BY
  5. Weekly refreshreviewed pull request
  1. Find every pricing term sheet (SEC form FWP) these companies filed, plus CoreWeave's 8-K disclosures for deals that never get one.
  2. A language model (Claude) reads each filing and extracts every tranche: amount, currency, coupon, maturity, price, yield, spread, identifiers, and a verbatim quote supporting the numbers.
  3. Deterministic checks reject anything suspicious: quotes must appear word for word in the filing; the stated spread must equal yield minus the Treasury benchmark within 5 basis points; the yield recomputed from price and coupon must match within 5 basis points. Failures go to a human review queue and are never published unreviewed.
  4. Pricing releases and closing filings for the same notes are merged so nothing is counted twice.
  5. Market data comes from FRED; company financials from the SEC's XBRL API; server lives from each 10-K, quoted in the data.

How accurate the extraction is

A second model, working only from the filings and blind to the pipeline's output, labelled 16 documents (87 tranches) as a gold set. The pipeline matches it on 100% of tranches, and on 100% of amounts, 100% of maturities, 100% of coupons and 100% of spreads. This check runs on every update; a miss fails the build.

References

  • Hart, O., and J. Moore (1994). A theory of debt based on the inalienability of human capital. Quarterly Journal of Economics 109(4), 841–879.
  • Myers, S. C. (1977). Determinants of corporate borrowing. Journal of Financial Economics 5(2), 147–175.
  • Stohs, M. H., and D. C. Mauer (1996). The determinants of corporate debt maturity structure. Journal of Business 69(3), 279–312.
  • Data: SEC EDGAR full-text and XBRL APIs; FRED series BAMLC0A0CM, BAMLC0A4CBBB, BAMLH0A0HYM2 (ICE BofA) and H.10 exchange rates; issuer 10-K reports as linked in the dataset.

Limits

  • Spreads are as priced at issue. Secondary-market prices (FINRA TRACE) have no free bulk feed.
  • Private credit and joint-venture financing are only visible where a company describes it in its own filings.
  • Useful lives are accounting estimates. Real hardware may last longer or shorter.
  • Cloud revenue is not in the SEC's XBRL API; it is read from each filing's segment tables, and Microsoft discloses Azure only as a growth rate.
  • The depreciation wave splits capex between servers and buildings by assumption; the companies do not disclose the split.
  • Interest expense is after capitalised interest, which flatters coverage for companies building heavily.

Use the data

  • bonds.csv every tranche, one row each
  • bonds.json same, with source quotes
  • metrics.json aggregates behind the charts
  • issuers.json financials and server lives
  • quarterly.json quarterly fundamentals, each value with its XBRL tag and filing
  • segments.json cloud segment revenue with quotes
  • commitments.json leases not yet commenced, with quotes

Definitions

Tranche
One series of notes, or one loan facility, within a deal.
Spread
Extra yield over a government bond of similar maturity, in basis points (1bp = 0.01%).
OAS
Option-adjusted spread: an index-wide spread that strips out the value of call options.
Useful life
The period over which a company depreciates an asset, its own estimate of how long the asset produces value.
FWP
Free writing prospectus: the final pricing term sheet filed with the SEC on the day a bond is sold.
DDTL
Delayed-draw term loan: a committed loan drawn down over time, used by CoreWeave to buy GPUs.

Every chart has an Embed button that gives you an iframe which updates with the data.
